bib.title: MEGABYTE: Predicting Million-byte Sequences with Multiscale Transformers

question: Can a multiscale decoder over byte patches model million-byte sequences end to end, matching subword models without tokenization at lower cost?
hypothesis: Most byte predictions are easy, so a small local model within patches plus a large global model across patches gives better performance per compute than a flat byte Transformer.
contributions: Multiscale decoder (patch embedder, global model, local model) with sub-quadratic attention, per-patch feedforward and parallel decoding
Compute- and data-controlled comparison against Transformer and PerceiverAR on text, image and audio
State-of-the-art-matching ImageNet 64x64 density estimation and 1.2M-byte image modelling

method.summary: Bytes are grouped into fixed patches of P; a patch embedder concatenates byte embeddings, a large global decoder-only transformer runs over patches, and a small local decoder predicts bytes within each patch conditioned on the global output. Compared to a Transformer and PerceiverAR in one codebase (Metaseq) with matched forward time per byte and equal bytes of training.
method.task: autoregressive byte-level language, image and audio modelling (next-byte prediction)

datasets.name: PG-19
datasets.source: Rae et al. 2019b, Project Gutenberg books before 1919

datasets.name: Code
datasets.source: open source code under Apache, BSD or MIT licenses

datasets.name: ImageNet (64x64, 256x256, 640x640)
datasets.preprocessing: 3 bytes per pixel; patch scan (p x p x 3 bytes, p = sqrt(P/3)) used by default; sequence lengths 12288, 196608, 1228800

datasets.name: Audio (Librilight-L referenced in ablation)
datasets.size: 2 TB, roughly 18,000 hours, 16 kHz 16-bit (32k bytes per second)
datasets.preprocessing: raw bytes read from file, 256 values

models.name: MEGABYTE (text, controlled)
models.architecture: two decoder-only transformers (global D=2048 L=14, local D=1024 L=18)

models.name: MEGABYTE (PG19 scaling / speed)
models.architecture: global D=2048 L=24, local D=1024 L=15

models.name: MEGABYTE (ImageNet64 SOTA)
models.architecture: global D=2560 L=32, local D=1024 L=24

models.name: PerceiverAR (byte)
models.architecture: decoder with one cross-attention over long context; own reimplementation

training.optimizer: Adam beta1=0.9 beta2=0.98, gradient clip max norm 1.0
training.lr: 2.00E-04 text (Table 12); 3.00E-04 for ImageNet64/640 baselines; 1.50E-04 for w/o local model arXiv ablation
training.lr_schedule: Metaseq polynomial decay to end LR 0
training.batch_size: varies per run: 48 (arXiv MEGABYTE), 72 (arXiv baselines), 2 (ImageNet64 SOTA), 32 (audio per Sec 7; 256 in Table 12), see Table 12
training.tokens: 80 billion bytes (controlled); 400B bytes (PG19 scaling); 1.4T tokens (ImageNet64 SOTA)
training.regularisation: pre-norm, ReLU activation; init normal mean 0 std 0.006 truncated at 2 std (Megatron-LM variant)
training.hardware: fairscale fully sharded model and optimizer states; GPU type and count not stated
training.compute: matched forward time per byte across architectures; absolute FLOPs/GPU hours not stated

other.note: Sec 7 gives audio batch size 32 while Table 12 gives 256 for audio MEGABYTE

inference.decoding: evaluation only (bpb); generation speed measured for 8192 bytes
inference.samples: single run per config; no seeds reported

parameters.strided inference: two forward passes offset by P/2, keep first half of each patch, 2X cost
parameters.sliding window: PerceiverAR eval stride = num latents/2; sliding/strided used only when comparing with prior work (Tables 3, 4) and in Table 8

metrics.name: word-level perplexity
metrics.definition: bpb converted to word-level for comparison with subword models

baselines: PerceiverAR (byte, own reimplementation reproducing 3.53 vs 3.54 bpb on ImageNet64)
TransformerXL, Compressive Transformer, PerceiverAR, BlockRecurrent (subword, reported)
eval.protocol: Compute- and data-controlled: layers adjusted to match forward time per byte, same bytes trained; no seeds or significance tests.

availability.code: Pseudocode in Appendix B; Metaseq used for training, MEGABYTE code link not stated
availability.data: public datasets except audio source not named

results.claim: MEGABYTE beats a compute-matched byte-level Transformer and PerceiverAR on all five text datasets (PG-19 bpb shown).
results.setup: Controlled: each model 80 billion bytes, same compute; Transformer 320M ctx 1024, PerceiverAR 248M ctx 8192, MEGABYTE 758M/262M global/local ctx 8192 patch 8

results.claim: On Code the MEGABYTE gap is largest.
At 400B bytes on PG-19, byte-level MEGABYTE reaches word-level test perplexity close to subword models.
results.baseline_value: 69.4 (byte Transformer), 88.8 (byte PerceiverAR); subword: TransformerXL 36.3, Compressive 33.6, PerceiverAR 28.9, BlockRecurrent 26.5
results.setup: PG-19, 400B bytes, compute matched to byte baselines; word-level conversion from bpb
results.note: Authors say comparison to subword models may be confounded by differing compute and tuning.

results.claim: MEGABYTE matches PerceiverAR state of the art on ImageNet 64x64 with about half the GPU hours.
results.setup: Global 2.7B / local 350M, 1.4T tokens; GPU hours estimated, not measured against a rerun
results.quote: MEGABYTE matches the state-of-the-art performance of PerceiverAR whilst using only half the compute.

results.claim: At 640x640 (1.2288M bytes) MEGABYTE beats compute-matched baselines in one forward pass.
results.setup: ImageNet640, equal GPU hours and data; Transformer ctx 1024, PerceiverAR ctx 12000 (per Sec 6.3), MEGABYTE full context patch 192
results.note: Sec 6.3 says PerceiverAR segment 12000, Table 12 lists 4,096 ctx with 1024 latents for Image640.

results.claim: MEGABYTE generates 8192 bytes 40% faster than a 350M Transformer despite over 4x parameters, with lower bpb.
results.setup: PG19, equal compute; MEGABYTE 1.3B global/218M local, ctx 8192 patch 8; Transformer 350M ctx 1024
results.note: Table 6 times are 132 s vs 93 s, a 29.5% cut in time, i.e. 1.42x throughput; 40% is the paper's wording.
results.quote: MEGABYTE also generates a sequence of 8192 tokens 40% faster than transformer

results.claim: Table 6 generation time and bpb for MEGABYTE.
results.table: Table 6, row MEGABYTE, column Generation Time (s)

results.claim: Raw audio from files: MEGABYTE has lower bpb than PerceiverAR and a vanilla Transformer.
results.setup: 2 TB (~18,000 hours) 16 kHz 16-bit audio, seq len 524,288, patch 32, batch 32
results.quote: Our model obtains bpb of 3.477, much lower than the results with perceiverAR (3.543) and vanilla transformer model (3.567).

Patch size is robust across a wide range on ImageNet256.

results.claim: Claimed attention cost O(N^(4/3)) with P = T^(1/3); FLOPs about 2T*mg/P when mg >> ml, allowing a P-times larger model for the same FLOPs.
In GPT3 architecture quadratic self-attention is only 1.4% of FLOPS; the intro says over 98% of FLOPS are position-wise feedforward.
results.setup: GPT3 architecture, estimate following Kaplan et al. 2020
results.quote: the quadratic self-attention computation accounts for only 1.4% of FLOPS

limits: Scale far below state-of-the-art LMs (authors: 'the scale of experiments here is far below those of state-of-the-art language models'); future work to scale up
Subword comparison in Table 3 is confounded by differing compute and tuning
Longer context (16,384) gave no further gain at this scale
No seeds, variance, hardware or GPU hours reported
Hyperparameters (patch size, ratio) tuned per modality; baselines are authors' own implementations
Text results are English only (plus code and LaTeX); no downstream tasks
